newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canada deports suspected Australian war criminal.
newsitem.headline: Canada deports suspected Australian war criminal.

text.p: Canada has ordered the deportation of an elderly Australian man accused of Nazi war crimes in Latvia during World War Two, Australian police said on Tuesday.
Konrad Kalejs, an 84-year-old Latvian who holds Australian citizenship, was deported from the United States in 1994 after a U.S. court ruled he was a Nazi officer in Latvia.
But Kalejs managed to remain in Canada en route to Australia, until the Canadian government sought to deport him on charges he was a war criminal and had falsely entered the country.

Australian Jews on Tuesday reacted angrily to news of Kalejs' likely return, calling on the government to reopen his case and prosecute Kalejs. Australian radio said he would be flying into Australia on Wednesday.

"I don't think any Australians want this country to be the dumping ground for war criminals, for someone that Canada and America don't want," said Jeremy Jones, vice-president of The Executive Council of Australian Jewry.

Australia Broadcasting Corp radio said Canadian immigration ordered Kalejs deported on Monday after ruling that while there was no evidence he personally brutalised anyone or ordered anyone to be brutalised, he was part of a system where brutality was carried out regularly.

"No one should be surprised Konrad Kalejs is being deported from Canada," Jones told Reuters. "The evidence against him that the Americans used to originally deport him was overwhelming. The person was a serious war criminal."
Kalejs, who denies being a Nazi officer but merely a university student, lived in Australia after the war and moved to the United States in 1959, before being deported in 1994.
A U.S. immigration judge ordered Kalejs deported because of his "assistance in Nazi persecution as a member of the notorious 'Arajs Kommando'" -- a Nazi death squad that operated in Latvia.
The squad has been charged with executing tens of thousands of Jews and gypsies.
Kalejs was allowed temporary entry to Canada after he was stopped at the airport by immigration officials in 1995. But he remained in the country.
Australia's war crimes unit, which was disbanded in 1993 after three failed prosecutions, investigated Kalejs but did not find grounds to prosecute.
The Australian Federal Police confirmed the Canadian decision and said the file on Kalejs remained open and his case would be reviewed.
"The AFP has sought access to material used in the Canadian proceedings," the AFP said in a statement.

"Following the review of all relevant material, the AFP will be in a position to decide, in conjunction with other law enforcement agencies, whether any offences have been committed by Mr Kalejs against Australian legislation."
Under Australia's War Crimes Act the government must prove under very strict burdens of proof that Kalejs participated in murder.

The Executive Council of Australian Jewry called on the government to change Australia's immigration laws to prevent suspected war criminals entering the country and to toughen laws dealing with war crimes.

"If it is found that despite the evidence that led him to be deported from Canada and America there is no grounds for prosecution, then I think that is a compelling reason for Australia to change our laws to allow us to deal with this case," Jones said.
"There is a huge difference between a country serving as a place of refugee or a place to build a new life and a country where you can be a fugitive from justice."
